newsitem.title: USA: GOLF-WOODS EYES HISTORIC MASTERS TRIUMPH.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-WOODS EYES HISTORIC MASTERS TRIUMPH.

text.p: Tiger Woods, on the brink of a breathtaking triumph in the Masters, was thinking beyond the birdies and eagles he used in his startling rush to dominance on golf's greatest stage.
He had history on his mind, the history of Augusta National as a whites-only club and the Masters as a tournament that shunned black players over the years.

Victory for the amazing 21-year-old Woods on Sunday, who signed endorsement deals worth $60 million when he turned pro last September, would mark the first major championship ever won by a man of colour.
It would come, ironically, two days before the 50th anniversary of Jackie Robinson's historic breaking of the colour line in baseball.

Woods, whose father is African-American and mother Asian- American, is poised to become the youngest Masters champion by turning a three-shot lead into a nine-stroke bulge on Saturday with a spectacular seven-under-par 65 that marked the second successive day he had posted the low round.
His dominance was palpable and his surge the golfing equivalent of Michael Jordan's explosive first step on the way to a jaw-dropping slam dunk.

Woods, whose prodigious length off the tee, golfer's imagination and mature short game has turned Augusta National into his own personal playground, paused to consider the reactions of some of the black golfers that came before him.
"I think they'll probably be going through several emotions," Woods said about the likes of Charles Sifford and Lee Elder, two early black professional golfers who have had an influence on him.

"I'm sure they wish it could have been them," Woods said Saturday. "But also I love those guys to death and they love me, and I know they are very proud of what I've done so far and hopefully tomorrow."
Elder was the first black player to compete in the Masters, qualifying for the 1975 tournament, the year of Woods's birth, by winning the 1974 Monsanto Open.

In 1972, the Masters adopted a rule to automatically invite players that won tournaments on the PGA Tour. Before then the Masters, as an invitational event, could pick and choose. Sifford won the Los Angeles Open in 1969 and was not invited.

Augusta National admitted its first black club member only after a row over racist club membership practices in golf that brought protests at the 1990 PGA Championship at Shoal Creek in Birmingham, Alabama.
Woods is aware of that history, and also of his own personal place in golf.
A golfing prodigy carefully nurtured by his father Earl, Woods became the youngest player to win the U.S. junior championship and later won an unprecedented three successive U.S. Amateur crowns.

"It means a lot, I guess for a number of reasons," Woods said about the prospects of adding a Masters green jacket to his wardrobe in his first try as a professional. "I would become the youngest to ever win."
On the importance of being first and youngest, Woods said: "That means a lot, because no one has ever accomplished that who's played the game. That means a lot to me.
"I mean, the Amateur has been played since 1894," he said, referring to his unique triple in that event. "That means a lot to me."

Woods has always been conscious of his place in golf history. He used to keep a chart on his bedroom wall listing the achievements of Jack Nicklaus, age by age, as a measuring stick for his own accomplishments.

"But I think, more importantly in my estimation, it's going to open up a lot of doors," he said about a Masters victory, "a lot of opportunities, and draw a lot of people into golf who never thought of playing the game.
"I think on this kind of stage and kind of media (attention), it's going to do a lot for the game as far as minority golf is concerned."
